title: BASS-II ReadMe
why: NASA's own explanation of the columns in the BASS-II test matrix, including the air-speed display.
paragraphs: Spreadsheets folder has test matrix and fan calibration information.
Test Matrix explanation
Tabs in spreadsheet for each PI.
Subrata Bhattacharjee burned various thickness of very thin pmma films.
Paul Ferkul burned Nomex III and a candle to round out the BASS-I testing.
Fletcher Miller burned various thickness and widths of thick pmma slabs (one sided and two sided burns).
Sandra Olson burned three sizes of pmma rods (mostly clear), igniting the upstream end for a stagnation flame / concurrent flow geometry.
Carlos Fernandez-Pello burned three sizes of pmma rods (mostly black), igniting the downstream end for an opposed flow flame spread geometry.
James T’ien burned mostly SIBAL fabric (75/25 cotton/fiberglass blend).  Also had 1 sample/2 tests with 4 cm pmma spherical section.
Columns in test matrix:
Date:  actual date of experiment.  Video display is one day later than actual date due to a leap year the on-board computer did not account for.
GMT- number is day of the year.  ISS runs on Greenwich mean time, so their clock reads as GMT – Year – Day - time
Test number:   Initial of PI name followed by test number from the initial matrix.   If multiple runs with same sample on same day, a and b are used to designate.
Sample number:   some samples were used for multiple runs.
Material:  self explanatory

Flow restrictors:  perforated plates that could be attached to the inlet screen to increase the flow restriction and thus reduce the flow range.   0 is highest flow, lowest restriction; and 2 is lowest flow, highest restriction.
Fan display:  instantaneous fan voltagex10 on the video display.  Maximum was 122, or 12.2 volts.  Also listed sometimes are pot settings on the control box.  10 is max.
Air display:  flow speed measured in the duct in cm/s on the video display.  Response time is very slow (~ 1 min), so reading is only steady for long times at the same flow setting.

Radiometer gain:   Uncalibrated radiometer gain, radiometer is displayed on the video.   Adjusted to avoid saturation.  Useful for relative flame intensity readings and flame dynamics (like pre-extinction oscillations).  Video display data rate is 5 Hz.
Total frames:  digital Nikon still image frames shot, includes test and post-burn sample images.
Calibrated initial and final O2:   The O2 sensor was out of calibration, so the MCA ISS reading was used to correct the initial ISS ‘air’ reading of the sensor for the day via a constant offset.
CO2 readings:  CDM sensor readings.
CO readings:  CSA-CP sensor readings.  OR = over range (> 1000 ppm)
Videos:   most test videos have the test number (PI initial+ # from test matrix)  In the Misc video folder, there are backup test recordings, recordings of crew operations, etc.

title: BASS-II fan calibration data
why: The air speed the duct reached at each fan setting. Its largest reading, 59 cm/s, is the ceiling used when the Air display column is read, and its fan display reads 38 with no air moving.

title: NASA's stated results for PSI-10
why: Results NASA states in its own reports, quoted in an evidence pack.
paragraphs: As expected in the normal-flame ISS testing, the flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration. (NTRS-20220005205.pdf, p. 7)

Very small flames have low radiative loss and asymptotically approach steady-state behavior, where one flame lasted over 14 minutes until it was terminated due to operational constraints. (NTRS-20220005205.pdf, p. 7)
In contrast, large flames increase in size over time until the flame extinguishes because of radiative heat loss. (NTRS-20220005205.pdf, p. 7)

Before extinction, these flames experience an unstable oscillatory mode, in which they partially quench and reform. The oscillations grow in magnitude until the flame fully extinguishes. (NTRS-20220005205.pdf, p. 7)
When ACME’s ISS testing ended in Feb. 2022, over 1,500 flames were ignited for its six experiments. (NTRS-20220005205.pdf, p. 8)

title: NASA's stated results for PSI-100
why: Results NASA states in its own reports, quoted in an evidence pack.
paragraphs: Saffire-III burned for 320 sec. (NTRS-20180005168.pdf, p. 16)
Saffire-I burned for 400 sec • Saffire-III burned for 320 sec. ♦This is equal to the inverse ratio of the flame speed (NTRS-20180005168.pdf, p. 16)
Flame spread over a large thin charring surface in low-gravity showed that steady flame spread was possible (unlike normal gravity). (NTRS-20180005168.pdf, p. 18)
Concurrent flame spread (with the wind) was shown to be more sensitive to the flow duct dimension than previously anticipated. (NTRS-20180005168.pdf, p. 18)
they determined that concurrent flames can achieve a steady spread rate and that overall the concurrent spread rates are strongly influenced the the flow duct size. (NTRS-20180005168.pdf, p. 20)

The comparatively much smaller diameters for the Kapton and Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices, on the other hand the large sizes seen with the lamp wick and silicone would generate very large signals on a light scattering system. (PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final Report.pdf, p. 5)

to have a system that would have the signal gain sensitive enough to trigger an alarm for the lower signal from small particles such as Teflon and Kapton without excessive nuisance alarms from large dust particles is difficult without some level of particle size discrimination. (PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final Report.pdf, p. 5)

These figures show a strong trend of increased particle size at low flow rates. This indicates that smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas. (PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final Report.pdf, p. 5)
The aging results show a substantial increase in the observed diameters. (PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final Report.pdf, p. 4)

For typical runs, the particle concentrations were a few million particles / cc and the mass concentrations were 2 to 15 mg/m3 however there were runs with fewer particles. (PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final Report.pdf, p. 4)
The repeatability of the diameter measurements is estimated to be +/- 15%. (PSI-101_Reports_SAME-R_Final Report.pdf, p. 5)

The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) examined the particle-size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft materials. These instruments can provide useful guidance for the designers of future spacecraft smoke detectors. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 26)

Fundamental research in microgravity highlighted the vastly different particulate size associated with flames in microgravity. Since many fire detectors operate by sensing fire-generated particulates, they would need to use different signatures to detect fires in microgravity. If terrestrial fire detectors were used in space, they would be “looking” for something different than they should. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 35)

title: NASA's stated results for PSI-107
why: Results NASA states in its own reports, quoted in an evidence pack.
paragraphs: The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins to emit soot. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 2)
Fifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 2)
Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 2)

Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 2)

The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 2)
The measured smoke point lengths were found to correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 2)

The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 2)

Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. The oxygen mole fraction of this cabin air is maintained within 19 – 24%. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 19)

The smoke point lengths, LSP, (and the flow conditions) were obtained from the video record and are the measured distance from the burner to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 19)
The luminous flame tips were not sharply defined in most images, but rather transitioned from bright yellow to black over an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 19)
Totally 526 flames were ignited and studied, which were much more than originally planned. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 20)
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel or air. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 20)

Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high air velocity, large burners, and long flames, and is attributed to coflow perturbations. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 20)
Smoke points were attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the copper plate at the end of the duct. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 20)
# smoke points 6 6 20 13 7 (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 20)
Parameters ua, uf, and Re assume conditions of 298 K, 101 kPa and 21±1% O2, and uniform velocity profiles. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 20)
For a given choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke point length. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 21)
Figure 18 reveals that smoke points of nonbuoyant coflowing flames decrease with increasing burner diameter. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 21)

The present smoke points generally were repeatable. An exception was the tests with the 0.41 mm burner (for which only propylene smoke points were possible). Testing on different days yielded different smoke points for this burner. (PSI-107_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf, p. 22)

The average spread rate over the 100-µm-thick sample in the normal-gravity experiments is found to be 2.0 mm/s (see Figure 2.19(b)). (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 48, printed page 40)
For the same fuel thickness, the highest spread rate obtained is about 2.2 mm/s (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 48, printed page 40)

Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition. (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 97, printed page 89)
Blowoff extinction limits from the ISS experiments agree well with Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop test limits. (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 97, printed page 89)
CO production also increases significantly at low O2 levels. The CO to CO2 ratio increases as well at low O2 concentrations. (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 97, printed page 89)

The quenching velocities are small (between 1 and 5 cm/s), and an accurate determination is necessary to resolve the slope of the quenching boundary. (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 109, printed page 101)

In general, the flames spread faster for two-sided burns compared to one-sided burns. The greater the thickness of the fuel, the greater is the time taken for the flame to spread and so the lower is the spread rate. (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 71, printed page 63)
This showed that most of the tests released well below 100 W. (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 19, printed page 11)

the global equivalence ratio for the tests is estimated to be 1.3 on average, which indicates the flames were burning fuel rich under the low-velocity forced-flow conditions. (PSI-25_Reports_BASS-II Summary Report.pdf, p. 19, printed page 11)

Quenching was observed when the flow became sufficiently weak that the flame could no longer provide adequate heat flux to compensate for the heat losses (conduction into the rod and radiation). (NTRS-20150008961.pdf, p. 1)
A surface energy balance is presented that shows the surface radiative loss exceeds the conductive loss into the rod near the limit. (NTRS-20150008961.pdf, p. 1)

For the blowoff branch, the boundary exhibits a linear dependence on oxygen concentration and stretch rate, indicating that the temperature at blowoff must be fairly constant. (NTRS-20150008961.pdf, p. 1)

the global equivalence ratio for the tests is estimated to be 1.3 on average, which indicates the flames were burning fuel rich under the low velocity forced flow conditions. (NTRS-20150019858.pdf, p. 9)

Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 samples did not burn on ISS atmosphere 21% to 22% O2 Flow speeds around 15 cm/s Similar to 1-g (Note: samples narrower on ISS) Nomex-III sample did burn (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 26)

Nomex III sample residue after nearly complete concurrent propagation at 15 cm/s on ISS. Flame was shrinking in width until it extinguished within 1 cm of the end of the sample, as its width became smaller than ~ 1 cm, which is on the scale of a fingering flamelet. (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 27)

Near the end of the burn, a jet of nitrogen is imposed but it fails to extinguish the flame. (Solid is very warm.) Finally after a series of flow reductions, the flame goes out when the flow speed is zero. Fuel: PMMA; 15-mm initial diameter; 17% O2/N2; 1 atm (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 52)
Nitrogen flow of 500 cc/min weakens but does not extinguish the flame (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 53)
Microgravity flames were found to be especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cm/s. (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 54)

At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cm/s) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable. However, heat loss at these very low convective rates is small so the flames can burn for a long time. (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 54)

At moderate flow speeds (between about 1 and 5 cm/s) the flame continually heats the solid fuel resulting in an increasing fuel temperature, higher rate of fuel vaporization, and a stronger, more luminous flame as time progresses. (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 55)
Thicker solids can store a great deal of heat even with only a small flame. One result is that extinction with the nitrogen jet was not possible for the given flow rate. (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 55)

Only the smallest flames burning acrylic slabs appeared to be adversely influenced by solid conductive heat loss, but even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing. (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 55)

This has implications for spacecraft fire safety since a tiny flame might be undetected for a long time. • While the small flame is not particularly hazardous if it remains small, the danger is that it might flare up if the air convection is suddenly increased or if the flame spreads into another fuel source. (NTRS-20140011099.pdf, p. 55)

Microgravity experiments demonstrated that the assumed margin of safety of reduced flammability in microgravity, based on quiescent test results, may not be valid for most spacecraft environments where ventilation flow strongly enhances flames. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 18)

In the low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity (Figure 8). (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 18)

Materials are easier to ignite in low gravity because of reduced natural convective cooling from the fuel surface. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 18)

Once established, flames in low-speed airflows may preferentially spread into the oncoming airflow (Figure 9) depending on the flow speed. This is opposite to the effect that occurs in normal gravity. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 18)

Radiant heat transfer was shown to substantially affect the material’s flammability. Surface radiative heat loss reduces the flammability, but an external radiative heat flux can cause materials to ignite and spread faster. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 18)

However, more recently nitrogen has been used to perform tests as low as 17 percent oxygen. The tests have yielded useful results on the flow-velocity effect and flame suppression (by nitrogen), and the quick return of the test results has helped to guide the next, more complete flight experiments. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 19)

Flame sequence of a burning 2-cm diameter acrylic sphere at 17 percent oxygen and 12 cm/s flow from the Burning and Suppression of Solids experiment. The images are about 1.5 sec. apart. With the reduction in oxygen from 21 percent (air) to 17 percent, the flame stays bluer much longer (soot formation is delayed) facilitating comparison with model. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 20)

Depending on the geometry of the flame and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle), it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen. Early results have demonstrated that nitrogen applied to the flame can actually strengthen it because of this effect. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 22)

This resulted in several critical misconceptions about potential fires in spacecraft: 1. A steady fire cannot exist in a quiescent microgravity environment. 2. A fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off. 3. Because the reduced-gravity environment is inherently safer, terrestrial fire standards and tests represent a very conservative approach to fire safety. Research at NASA GRC in both ground-based laboratories and microgravity facilities and space-based microgravity experiments (summarized by Friedman and Ross, 2001 and Ruff et al., 2009) demonstrates the fallacy of these assumptions and demonstrates GRC’s contribution to spacecraft fire safety science with respect to fire prevention through material flammability and screening. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 35)

title: NASA's stated results for PSI-47
why: Results NASA states in its own reports, quoted in an evidence pack.
paragraphs: The three tests that sampled the undisturbed environment in the ISS showed very low levels of airborne particulates, averaging fewer than 0.005 mg/m3 from the DustTrak® and fewer than 15 particles/cm3 from the P-Trak® (these are typical readings at the baseline). (PSI-47_Presentations_Daft_FactSheet.pdf, p. 2)

The three tests that sampled the undisturbed environment in the ISS showed very low levels of airborne particulates, averaging fewer than 0.005 mg/m3 from the DustTrak® and fewer than 15 particles/cm3 from the P-Trak® (these are typical readings at the baseline). (PSI-47_Presentations_Daft_FactSheet.pdf, p. 2)
These numbers are dramatically lower than the values recorded in the Space Shuttle in an earlier experiment (~ .050 mg/m3). (PSI-47_Presentations_Daft_FactSheet.pdf, p. 2)

Overall, the readings from these instruments are almost an order of magnitude below those that would normally be seen in a typical laboratory environment (~ 4,000 – 6,000 pt/cc for P-Trak), but were not totally unexpected, due to the presence of a HEPA filter on the ISS air handling system. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section II.D.1 (DAFT-1 & DAFT -2, Session 1, GMT 54, 2005))

Test point #1 data (Figures 1 and 2) shows that the overall particulate levels in the US Lab atmosphere are very low, about a factor of ten leaner than normal US office conditions. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))

Test point #2 data (Figures 3 and 4) shows that the P-Trak responded to the Velcro dust quite well, with several readings above the 30,000 pt/cc mark (P-Trak has a maximum count of 500,000 pt/cc). (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))
DustTrak also responded well to the Velcro dust, but did not reach readings above 10% of its overall capability. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))
Test points #3 and #4 were not appreciably different from Test point #1 for either device. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))

Overall, in the 1-g testing scenario, the particulate levels drop together with time, consistent with gravitational rainout of the particles in the sample bag. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))

The data points are clustered to the left of the line (area), in a region where the count/mass ratio is lower than what was determined from ground testing. This indicates then, that the mass of the average particle counted on-orbit is higher than that determined on Earth. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))

This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))

It should be noted that, although the DAFT Impactor is designed to filter out the larger particles, it is only about 50% efficient; which implies that it is allowing a considerable number of larger particles to be drawn into the devices. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))
The average mass (assuming a material density of water) is 2.5 E-12 grams, with a range from 2 – 3 E-12. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))
The calculated average diameter is 1.65 micron, ranging from 1.56 – 1.7 micron. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))
Therefore, the net amount of sample delivered to the Sample Bags is about 25 milligrams. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.B (Completeness/Quality of Data))

It also shows that as the run time on the P-Trak is increasing, especially during Bag #3, the count/mass ratio is declining. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.F (Final Investigation results))

However when the Ptrak and Dusttrak were returned, the data sets were intact in their memory. The stored data reproduced the read downs very closely giving confidence to the earlier conclusions. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.F (Final Investigation results))

The project team believes that the optimal reading range for the P-Trak is from 30,000 – 100,000 pt/cc (although the published range goes up to 500,000 pt/cc) and for the DustTrak; 20 – 80 mg/m3. Clearly, the latest data was within this range. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.F (Final Investigation results))

The data shows that the devices were able to operate in microgravity for an extended period of time with no apparent failure. One of the major concerns was that the P-Trak would accumulate alcohol in the optics chamber and obscure them, causing the unit to either read ‘0’ or display and error code. This did not happen. The units gave readings from zero well up into the middle of their operational ranges, and then back; in short, they performed as expected. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.F (Final Investigation results))

DAFT-1 and -2 showed that the units were ‘apparently working’ and that the air aboard the ISS is almost unbelievably clean. The readings from the devices during that part of the overall experiment though, never crossed the 20% of the operational range threshold, leaving the results somewhat suspect. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.F (Final Investigation results))
Due to the constraints listed above, DAFT-4, using the ‘unmodified’ P-Trak, was not performed. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.F (Final Investigation results))
The DAFT experiment adequately demonstrated the reliability of the modified Ptrak as operated in low-gravity. (PSI-47_Reports_DAFT_FinalReport.doc, section III.G (Conclusion))

Spacecraft fire detection provides significant challenges compared to terrestrial conditions because the properties of the smoke emitted from fires is affected by buoyancy. The conditions on a spacecraft require rapid detection of fires with limited false alarms. Two recent experiments examined the issues related to spacecraft fire detection. The Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test examined the background aerosol particulate levels on the ISS. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 26)

title: NASA's stated results for PSI-69
why: Results NASA states in its own reports, quoted in an evidence pack.
paragraphs: During the assembly of the MDCA hardware, a conformal coating was applied to the fuel-dispensing needles. The product was applied in two layers, a primer (Dow Corning 1204) and a conformal coat (Dow Corning 3140 RTV (MIL–A–46146) coating). Subsequent testing showed that the coating can both dissolve and “flake” off in both methanol and heptane. When this occurred, the deployed fuel droplet was clearly not pure but contained an unknown amount of the conformal coating. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 22)

Burning-rate constants were average, and the droplet history was minimally influenced by the contaminant. The contaminant was likely present in trace amounts and was a very low volatility compound. Because methanol and heptane are relatively high volatility fuels, the droplet regression history was dominated by the fuel not by the contaminant. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 23)
Disruptive extinction of methanol is probably due to the presence of the contaminant. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 23)

Disruptive extinction of heptane may be due to the presence of the contaminant. Subsequent tests with clean needles and fuel, however, also exhibited disruptive extinction at small droplet sizes, so no conclusion can be drawn regarding disruptive burning for heptane in the tests reported herein. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 23)
The diffusive extinction droplet diameters (smaller diameters) for methanol (where there is no disruption) were minimally influenced by the presence of the contaminant. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 23)
Radiative extinction droplet diameters (larger diameters) were not influenced by the presence of the contaminant. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 23)

In each test, there is a clear ambiguity in the droplet size during ignition (after deployment and before the igniters withdraw). This was the result of the broadband glow from the igniters changing the discrimination between the droplet and the background. This was especially present from the FLEX– 001 test to the FLEX–009 test. For these tests, the shutter speed (integration time of the array) was 1/30 s (inverse of the framing rate). After the FLEX–009 test, the shutter speed decreased to a much smaller value (1/1000 s) with a corresponding increase in the illumination level. This minimized the image distortion caused by the igniters and the broadband flame radiation (from soot for heptane), resulting in more accurate droplet size data. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 22)

The flame diameters from the color camera are typically about three-fourths of those from the LLUV camera. This discrepancy is not unusual and is a result of the LLUV being sensitive to the OH• chemiluminescence, which typically peaks outside of the visible flame. For heptane tests, where there is significant soot luminosity (which is not visible in the LLUV, but dominates the color camera), the discrepancy is even larger because the peak of the soot luminosity is typically inside the blue flame envelope. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 22)

Histories of droplet and flame diameters, as well as burning- rate constants and extinction diameters, were obtained in Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) program experiments performed on the International Space Station for methanol and n-heptane droplets with initial diameters between 2 and 5 mm. Burning was done in oxidizing atmospheres at ambient temperature and at various pressures between 0.70 and 3.05 atm, over ranges of dilution of oxygen with nitrogen, oxygen with carbon dioxide, and mixtures thereof. The experimental methods and data analysis procedures are reported here, and the results are presented and catalogued. More than 100 useful combustion histories were obtained. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 23)

The MDCA provided two radiometers: a broadband radiom- eter to detect the total radiative output of the flame and a radiometer with a filter to examine the emission from the water vapor. For the tests reported herein, these radiometers were not sensitive enough to provide reliable quantitative information about flame radiometric output, so the data are not reported. (NTRS-20150023456.pdf, p. 10)

The research to date has shown that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity. The implication is that terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in low gravity do not offer the same margin of safety as in normal gravity. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 12)

The FLEX experiments performed to date demonstrated radiative and diffusive extinction, combustion instabilities, lower flammability limits and recently explained cool flame phenomenon after visible flame extinction. Comparison with theoretical and numerical models validated aspects of the models while identifying areas that require improvement. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 13)

Inexplicably after hot flame extinction, however, the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period and then suddenly stopped vaporizing at a finite droplet size. The plateau in vaporization occurred coincident with the formation of a large vapor cloud. This vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 33)

Cool flames form as an intermediate step between unreacted fuel and oxidizer, but should not form after a hot flame extinguishes. The FLEX tests showed that the cool flame can burn for a prolonged period of time. (PSI-20_Science Documents_ISS_Researchers_Guide_-_Combustion_In_Reduced_Gravity.pdf, p. 34)
